comparison: Both address anti-drift performance claims (C3, C31, C44, C45). OpenEval finds these claims SUPPORTED by quantitative results in Figures 2A-E. Peer reviewers also acknowledge this as the 'major strength of the paper' with 'solid' evidence, explicitly confirming ADPT's reduced keypoint jumps compared to existing methods.

Both evaluate cross-species performance claims (C60, C65-C68). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED with clear quantitative advantages. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning whether performance differences are meaningful, noting that ADPT and DeepLabCut 'look identical' in Figure 5B with overlapping uncertainty bars despite claims of superiority.

Both address identity recognition claims (C4, C73). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by 93.16% accuracy results. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about validation methodology with limited dataset (10 mice, only 2 in same arena) and potential data leakage if training/validation frames were temporally interspersed.

Both evaluate temporal correction claims (C74, C75). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by dramatic improvement from 90.36% to 99.72%. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN as part of broader identity recognition validation concerns, questioning whether the validation setup reflects realistic use cases.

Both address multi-animal tracking claims (C33, C76-C80). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by quantitative results in Figure 8C-F with substantial improvements. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, explicitly criticizing lack of proper multi-animal validation, noting poor pose estimation in actual videos and absence of comparison with DLC/SLEAP multi-animal modes.

Both evaluate inference speed claims (C6, C69). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED but notes hardware specifications should be stated. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning whether different image sizes were used for training vs. validation (half size vs. 1288x964) and whether characterizing 90±4 fps as 'equivalent' to 106±4 fps is appropriate.

Both address ablation study claims (C61, C63, C70, C71, C81). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED though notes modest improvements (0.2-0.4%). Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, with no specific critique of these architectural validation experiments, implicitly endorsed by editor's 'solid' evidence assessment.

Both evaluate robustness claims (C52-C55). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by ANOVA results in Figure 3A-D demonstrating independence from confounding factors. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, acknowledging 'remarkable anti-drift performance, cross-individual and cross-view capabilities' as part of demonstrated single-animal efficacy.

Both address architecture design claims (C30, C36, C37, C84, C102-C105). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate technical detail and citations. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting 'a number of places where what was actually done wasn't clear,' specifically questioning deconvolution implementation details across branches.

OpenEval addresses cross-species validation (C32, C56-C59) finding SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers' R1 partially overlaps (C56, C57) as part of broader anti-drift performance acknowledgment, finding this aspect SUPPORTED as contributing to the 'major strength' of single-animal pose estimation.

OpenEval evaluates StanfordExtra dataset performance (C72) finding SUPPORTED with detailed PCK breakdown by body part. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific dataset validation.
OpenEval evaluates data efficiency claims (C62) finding SUPPORTED but notes 'acceptable performance' is subjectively defined. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific claim.

OpenEval evaluates marmoset dataset performance (C82, C83) finding SUPPORTED though notes ADPT's advantage is less pronounced. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this cross-species validation.
